title: Thoughts on knowledge
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino extends her earlier writing on schemas by sketching four ways a piece of knowledge links to others. Taking a core fact, surface area in Biology, she distinguishes sequential knowledge (what comes directly before and after in the teaching sequence), planar knowledge (related background such as cells and adaptations), tangential knowledge (links across topics or subjects such as rates of reaction) and layered knowledge (increasing detail over years). She notes that teaching a fact stripped of context lets students regurgitate it without anything to build on. Her practical conclusion is that planning needs to situate new knowledge within existing knowledge and an idea of where it leads, and she plans to make tangential and layered links more explicit.
points: Castelino offers a simple vocabulary for how a core fact connects: sequential, planar, tangential and layered knowledge.
Teachers typically plan for sequential links, but planar and tangential links also matter for understanding.
Layering shows knowledge gaining resolution from primary to secondary, as adaptations deepen over years.
Context-free facts can be recited but not built on, so teaching should locate knowledge in existing knowledge and its future use.
quotes: Lets say you have a bit of knowledge you want to teach your students. We will call this the core fact. For example: the concept of surface area in Biology. This dot represents this knowledge.

The obvious next step is the sequence of knowledge that our core fact sits within. We can call this sequential knowledge. The arrow shows the sequence in which the core fact fits in. Directly related knowledge came before it and will follow the core fact. In this case, before the core fact, students will have been taught about cell transport. Following teaching surface area, students will move on to transport systems. One leads to the next and each is needed to more along the sequence.

However, there are several important pieces of knowledge that are important and linked to the core fact, even if they are not directly related within the sequence. For instance, with surface area, students need to be know about cells in general (what are the different sub-cellular structures, what are specialised cells) and will move on to adaptations eventually. We can call this planar knowledge

But there is also knowledge that links with our core fact but is not part of the sequence in either direction. We can call this tangential knowledge. In our example of surface area, a piece of tangential knowledge may be the effect of surface area on homeostasis in organisms or, in Chemistry, how surface area of particles can affect their rate of reaction. These pieces of knowledge are definitely linked but not in an obvious sequence.

Teaching a key fact devoid of context and meaning may mean that our students can regurgitate it later but have no understanding that they can build on. This is widely agreed on but part of providing the context is to situate the new knowledge within existing knowledge and having an idea of where it will lead.
